items.readable_text:
Content:
We need to recognize when a particular series looks like a standard Maclaurin series. A list of some common Maclaurin series is given below.

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x^{2} + ⋯ + x^{n} + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)x^{n},|x ∈ (− 1, 1); (1)/(1 + x) = 1 − x + x^{2} − ⋯ + (− 1)^{n}x^{n} + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)(− 1)^{n}x^{n},|x ∈ (− 1, 1); e^{x} = 1 + x + (1)/(2!)x^{2} + ⋯ + (x^{n})/(n!) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)(x^{n})/(n!),|x ∈ (− ∞, ∞); \ln (1 + x) = x − (1)/(2)x^{2} + (1)/(3)x^{3} − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n + 1}x^{n})/(n) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n + 1}x^{n})/(n),|x ∈ (− 1, 1]; \sin (x) = x − (1)/(3!)x^{3} + (1)/(5!)x^{5} + ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)((− 1)^{n}x^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!),|x ∈ (− ∞, ∞); \cos (x) = 1 − (1)/(2!)x^{2} + (1)/(4!)x^{4} − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n})/((2n)!) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)((− 1)^{n}x^{2n})/((2n)!),|x ∈ (− ∞, ∞)]

Content:
In this lesson, we will focus on recognizing the standard Maclaurin series for the sine and cosine functions.

Content:
Note: To remember the series for [MATH: \sin x] and [MATH: \cos x] easily, notice that they are both alternating series that contain every other term of the expansion for [MATH: e^x.] Sine has the odd-degree terms (since it is an odd function), and cosine has the even-degree terms (since it is an even function).

sections.readable_text: What is the sum of the series [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{(\pi/3)^3}{3!} + \dfrac{(\pi/3)^5}{5!}-\cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n}(\pi/3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+\cdots\,?]

sections.normalized_html:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for [MATH: f(x) = \sin x.]

[MATH: \sin x|= x − (x^{3})/(3!) + (x^{5})/(5!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯]

Substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}] into our Maclaurin expansion gives

[MATH: \sin ((π)/(3))|= (π)/(3) − ((π/3)^{3})/(3!) + ((π/3)^{5})/(5!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}(π/3)^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯; (sqrt(3))/(2)|= (π)/(3) − ((π/3)^{3})/(3!) + ((π/3)^{5})/(5!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}(π/3)^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯.]

Therefore, the sum of the series is [MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

items.title: Recognizing Series That Are Similar to the Maclaurin Expansion for Cosine

sections.normalized_html:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for [MATH: f(x) = \cos x.]

[MATH: \cos x = 1 − (1)/(2!)x^{2} + (1)/(4!)x^{4} − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n})/((2n)!) + ⋯]

Substituting [MATH: x=3] into our Maclaurin expansion gives

[MATH: \cos (3)|= 1 − (3^{2})/(2!) + (3^{4})/(4!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}3^{2n})/((2n)!)⋯; \cos (3)|= 1 − (9)/(2!) + (81)/(4!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}3^{2n})/((2n)!)⋯.]

Therefore, the sum of the series is [MATH: \cos(3).]

Item 2 — Example: Recognizing Series That Are Similar to the Maclaurin Expansion for Sine

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for [MATH: f(x) = \sin x.]

[MATH: \sin x|= x − (x^{3})/(3!) + (x^{5})/(5!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯]

Substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}] into our Maclaurin expansion gives

[MATH: \sin ((π)/(3))|= (π)/(3) − ((π/3)^{3})/(3!) + ((π/3)^{5})/(5!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}(π/3)^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯; (sqrt(3))/(2)|= (π)/(3) − ((π/3)^{3})/(3!) + ((π/3)^{5})/(5!) − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}(π/3)^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯.]
